The decay distance of $B^0_s\rightarrow K^+K^-$ particles was studied, analyzing 6.0 pb^{-1} of data from the LHCb detector at the CP2 energy.  Two methods were used to determine the lifetime of these particles, yielding nearly identical outcomes.  The first method, based on the end-point, gave a mean transit distance of 275+14-13 \mu m with 14% total uncertainty.  The second, employing a maximum-likelihood approach, provided the transverse decay-time distribution, from which the $B^0_s$ lifetime was calculated as 0.891+0.019-0.018 ps, with 2.1% total uncertainty.  The most precise $B^0_s\rightarrow K^+K^-$ lifetime measurement to date, a figure of merit of 0.079 was achieved.  This value can be directly compared to other precise lifetime measurements to validate the test of lepton-universality in the ratio $\Gamma (B^0_s\rightarrow D^0\mu^+ \mu^-)/\Gamma (B^0_s\rightarrow D^0e^+ e^-)$.  The $B^0_s$ lifetime derived from this data, gave a figure of merit of 0.891+0.019-0.018 ps

Our analysis of high-energy recorded events from the Pierre Auger Observatory surface station reveals significant anisotropies at energies exceeding 4 Exa-electron volts. By correlating event data with the NEDMap 3.0 all-sky map of the night sky, we discovered a notable anisotropy in event distribution when observing a 100 Exa-electron volts event sample. Specifically, events from the Southern Hemisphere exhibit a 25% greater probability of occurrence compared to those from the Northern Hemisphere, representing a 4.2 sigma discrepancy that surpasses both geometric and muonic composition expectations. This event altitude difference exhibits energy dependence, increasing from 21% at 100 Exa-electron volts to 30% at 4 Exa-electron volts. Additionally, we detected an anisotropy in event direction relative to nearby quasars, resulting in a 19% higher event probability in the direction of bright nearby quasars beyond 4 Exa-electron volts. These findings are inconsistent with the observed rigidity spectrum and indicate that low-rigidity events are more susceptible to anisotropy than high-rigidity events.

The ATLAS detector at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) enabled researchers to study a variety of charged particle features in p+Pb interactions. These analyses were conducted by an ATLAS working group using a rich dataset collected during 2013 and 2016 runs, spanning a wide range of multiplicities. They also compiled nuclear modification factors for p+Pb and p+p collisions, providing essential reference material for the interpretation of data from the ATLAS detector during RIKEN's upcoming heavy-ion collider tests. Furthermore, they examined charged particle relationships with the LHC's findings on hydrodynamic behavior, reporting results on particle spectra, momentum distribution, and particle-type ratios, including the abundance of photons. This wealth of information will aid in modeling hadronic outcomes and support the assessment of charged particle distributions in p+Pb collisions as a benchmark for future experiments at the Heavy Ion Linear Collider (HILC).

The study of time-evolution in quantum dynamical systems on finite-dimensional noncommutative spaces is discussed, with a focus on those that admit a star-product representation and are invariant under a Lie symmetry, with applications in physics considered.

A crucial component in predicting a cancer patient's survival is the precise classification of tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes into three major types - large granular lymphocytes, neutrophils, and other white blood cells. This study aims to develop a framework for training models to identify and categorize these cells within patches of cancer tissue. Our proposed framework utilizes a federated learning approach, which enables the training of models across multiple institutions without the need to share patient data. We evaluated this framework by training models at five different sites and assessing their ability to classify cells when tested at those same sites as well as two additional ones. The results showed that our federated learning approach outperformed local training models and achieved an overall accuracy of 98.9% in classifying cells.

Underwater communications using nano and pico Watts of power require highly sensitive Decision-Feedback Equalizers (DFEs) to overcome signal degradation caused by underwater propagation. However, the random microbubbles that form in water can create substantial bubbles that rapidly scatter and pop, generating acoustic bursts of noise that can drastically reduce communication performance or even make it impossible, particularly in the low-power regime where signals are already significantly attenuated. As a solution, a novel, unusual technique called acoustic optical phase-shift keying (AOPSK) modulations takes advantage of the formation of microbubbles by inducing the bubbles to change the polarization state of a transmitted, low-power, linearly polarized optical signal. This new method enables more stable and reliable communication in underwater environments with attenuated signals distorted by noise. A field trial was conducted in a 200-meter underwater channel to test and validate the feasibility of this new technique in practice.

In Time-scaled Network Pruning for Temporal convolutions (TNT) is a network structure optimizer designed for Temporal Convolutional Networks (TCNs). TCNs have emerged as a prominent architecture in time-series modeling and can achieve superior performance compared to Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) when a large number of filters are utilized. TCNs features Temporal Dilated Convolution (TDC) blocks consisting of multiple standard convolutional layers, leading to high parameter counts that hinder their deployment on resource-constrained devices. TNT introduces a new network optimization approach called Trimming In Time (PIT) to maintain the performance of TCNs while significantly reducing parameters and computational complexity. The PIT module consists of a set of time-related operations to automatically determine the optimal temporal dilated dilations (TDR) and prune standard convolutional layers in TDC blocks. The PIT module is seamlessly integrated into TCNs and trainable, allowing for a fair comparison of parameters and computational complexity. Experimental results demonstrate that the PIT module outperforms current TCNs parameter reduction techniques and achieves 97 macs/sec/$\mu$s and 95 macs/sec/$\mu$s in time-series forecasting and classification tasks respectively, after making the parameters of TCNs comparable.

It has been proven that all Zinbiel algeres are solvable. Furthermore, a specific subclass of Zinbiel algebras, denoted as $g$, has been identified which when direct sums with other Zinbiel algebras maintain the property of being isomorphic to nil-Zinbiel algebras. It further finds that this subclass $g$ is itself a nil-Zinbiel algebra and so do all algebras within this subclass.

Our analysis of one-dimensional and two-dimensional spectra from the LHC, obtained from Pb-Pb collisions at a high energy of $\sqrt{s_{\rm NN}}$ = 5.02 TeV, involved an examination of the average lead azimuthal angle, denoted as $\langle \phi \rangle_{\rm lead}$, for the particle types of protons, $\pi^+$, and $p_\textrm{T}^{\rm max}$ for particles with a mass less than one GeV/c$^2$, and the nucleus of the lead. We found variations in both $\langle \phi \rangle_{\rm lead}$ and $p_\textrm{T}^{\rm max}$ as they relate to the initial Pb-Pb collision geometry. Specifically, we observed that $\langle \phi \rangle_{\rm lead}$ for both protons and $\pi^+$, and $p_\textrm{T}^{\rm max}$, vary in response to an initial Pb-Pb collision geometry, providing insights into the lead intensity and the overall dynamics of the collision.

The concept of double layered lattices (DLLs) was first proposed by A. A. Saloun in 2009. Building on this foundation, various extensions of double layered lattices have been developed, each focusing on different aspects. In 2015, A. A. Saloun and A. K. Ghatak introduced the theory of DLE-logics, a first-order logic system that utilizes double layered signatures and interprets formulas within the context of DLEs. This system has since led to the derivation of numerous important results, particularly in the area of monadic DLE-logics, where the local finiteness property has been established for algebras of these logics. The work presented here extends the concepts of dualities found in ALFs and FLs to DLLEs, resulting in the development of dualities for DLEs and their associated algebras. These new frameworks have further implications for DLE-logics, allowing for the generalization of previously discovered results. Specifically, the dualities presented here enable the proof of an inverse representation theorem for DLEs and their associated DLE-logics.

Deterministic functions form a crucial basis for data management and have been used to create integrity constraints like referential integrity. These rules can be seen as a type of functional dependency and can be applied to relational tables. Researchers have also explored them in the context of partial tables to develop synthesis algorithms for dependency preservation. A significant challenge in practical data processing is handling incomplete tables, which often contain missing values. This issue can be addressed by extending tables with null entries. Another approach is to distinguish between different kinds of functional relations, such as those used in query rewriting and table cleaning algorithms. This investigation focuses on characterizing consistency in tables with missing values and prescribes the conditions under which a table is correct according to a given set of functional relations. This study also explores how different types of functional relations impact characterizations of table consistency.

For a diverse range of applications, count-based time series models have seen a significant rise in complexity, for instance, in modeling neural spike activity. Existing methods, including GARCH-type count time series models, have been developed up to the frequency of single sample intervals. In contrast, we introduce a novel TV-PAR model that captures the intensity function in continuous time, accounting for cyclical patterns. We outline the TV-PAR model's mathematical underpinnings, prove its stability and stationarity, and outline the HOSCP properties. For parameter estimation, a marginal likelihood-based approach is proposed, and a Gaussian approximation for the marginal likelihood is derived. The TV-PAR model's viability is demonstrated through extensive simulations and an empirical analysis of GDP growth data.

This paper introduces Description Fields (DFs), a novel way to represent 3D objects that overcomes significant challenges in current methods. Many existing approaches struggle with high-dimensional data, creating robust sets of point clouds, and processing unstructured input. DFs consist of continuous voxel grids describing object properties like surface location, color, and physical behavior. Due to their structure, neural networks can process anything from sparse data to full 3D models, extracting descriptions of objects. Current object representation methods often rely on flattening point clouds for efficiency, but this loses critical spatial information. Due to the inherent point clouds in DFs, tasks like shape analysis, set estimation, and processing are handled natively, making DFs a breakthrough in object representation technology.

The concept of the SiD detector has been the innermost part of the ICSCRD design for over a decade. However, with the decision to upgrade to CLICCL, new considerations are being made regarding its inner components, specifically the SiD detector. This detector would have a unique triangular layout and an innovative design, but to reduce construction costs and better match the timing of other detectors, a modified SiD-2 detector has been proposed. This modified detector would have two layers of sensors and a more compact inner design, which would have significant implications for the detection of charged particles and lepton identification. This design would also require a new and upgraded magnetic field system, which would have further effects on the detector's performance. This document provides detailed calculations and simulations for the modified SiD-2 detector's design and its impact on the detection of particles.

We examined the stellar composition of red giant stars in two bright segments of the globular cluster Tonantzintla 2, located in the Milky Way's central bulge. By using high-resolution spectra, we determined their ages, chemical makeup, and spin speeds. The cluster's stars are estimated to be between 9.0 to 10.0 billion years old, with a chemical composition similar to that of metal-poor external halo clusters. The cluster exhibits a gradient in nitrogen abundance, with narrower cores showing higher nitrogen levels than the outer regions, a feature observed in some other bulge and thick disk clusters. The study also revealed moderate spin rates in the cluster's core (around 150 m/s) but lower spin speeds in the outer regions (around 60 m/s), which may indicate a more massive inner core. These findings support previous research suggesting that certain bulge clusters with similar properties to Tonantzintla 2 may have contributed to the formation of the Milky Way's central bar and supermassive black hole.

As proof ideas become more intricate in theorem-proving, increasing reliance on library components may hinder efficiency. A framework comprising lemmas and theorems, paired with a formalized structure of dependencies, can improve clarity and facilitate customization for specific applications. This paper introduces and analyzes the concept of a framework within the context of the Isabelle Archive of Formal Proofs, investigating the existing contents, conducting a comprehensive examination, and proposing a design for implementation. The study also presents initial efforts to integrate this concept into specific domains, while providing the source code for the proposed methodology on GitHub.

This study seeks to identify the specific place of Yang-Lee edge criticality (YLCC) within the standard O(N) universality class on a triangular lattice. Using a statistical analysis of the zero-energy sector of the Heisenberg spin chain, we examined traditional (T) and non-standard (NT) Yang-Lee Ising models (TLI and NTLI). Through TLI and NTLI, we can derive the standard and non-standard critical Yang-Lee points respectively. By evaluating order parameter susceptibility, we found that both standard and non-standard YLCC belong to the O(2) traditional universality class.

In 2018, a significant finding demonstrated the local convexity of the TAP free energy within a sufficient threshold of a randomness parameter, indicating the applicability of convex optimization techniques to analyze the TAP equations' dynamics and convergence. This particular outcome was initially established for a narrow range of model parameters. We have recently made an advancement by extending this result to a broader parameter set, including instances of the Gaussian and Bernoulli random matrix ensembles. Another key contribution involves the development of a measure concentration phenomenon that concentrates around the Hessian of a convex function. We anticipate that this concentration measure could find applications in proving the existence and concentration of solutions that are relevant to the Spherical Model.

This computational examination provides a metasurface model based on electric and magnetic polarizabilities, offering a straightforward and versatile framework for rapidly assessing complex, non-linear interactions between light and three-dimensional objects with integrated metasurfaces. By simplifying the problem to two dimensions, we successfully evaluate a range of nonlinear effects, including harmonic generation, surface-dependent response, and light-induced light interaction, even with limited degrees of freedom, and verify our findings with three-dimensional simulations and experiments. This framework is readily applicable to any periodic structure and can be utilized to design customized nonlinear optical devices.

The primary objective of this research is to verify the conjecture that every smooth, totally integrable vector field with a non-degenerate singular point and no periodic orbits can have a linearizable singular point. Additionally, we will provide an proof for the case of plane vector fields and gather relevant information for the case of space vector fields.

Although the Complete Configuration Interaction method produces precise numerical solutions for molecular properties, it becomes computationally unfeasible for all but the most basic systems. To circumvent this limitation, a complementary approach has been proposed, where CI values are derived for individual molecular degrees of freedom and combined to predict other properties. However, this approach is hindered by a significant discrepancy between the 1D one-electron calculations and the complex reality of interacting electrons. In an effort to bridge this gap, a computational model was trained to generate accurate CI values and subsequently used to calculate various molecular properties. The results showed that the deep learning model could produce correct predictions for properties such as CI values, correlation energy, ionization energy, and electron attachment, even when applied to completely new molecules.

Yolo City Cluster in the sky contains a massive cluster of galaxies spanning 2.5 million light years, with a striking feature discovered within. This massive curve, with a diameter of 600,000 light years, is composed of numerous galaxies, likely remnants of past collisions between the main cluster and adjacent smaller clusters. This discovery provides valuable evidence for the dynamic processes that shape galaxy clusters, and further research could shed light on the evolution of these cosmic structures.

The search for extraterrestrial life relies on the detection of planetary anomalies or signals in the electromagnetic spectrum, where the contribution from a host star's atmosphere, including the aether, significantly hampers the desired data.  To tackle this challenge, our research proposes the utilization of photometric data from interstellar matter and the aether as indicative of their compositional characteristics, providing valuable information about potential life forms.  To investigate the potential contents of interstellar matter and the aether, we use the statistics of stellar brightness variations, specifically focusing on the Gaia dataset to demonstrate the feasibility of extracting detailed information about these components through statistical analysis.  Our findings reveal the ability to gather novel data about interstellar matter and the aether, which can be applied to the detection of exoplanets and potentially life forms in the future.  Furthermore, our suggestions for utilizing deep learning techniques to extract detailed information about interstellar matter and the aether from data will aid in the detection of exoplanets and life signs in the future.

This paper enhances our prior work on DeepHMap, a novel approach for robust pose estimation in any direction for mobile robots using place recognition. Our method initially creates a holistic, high-resolution orientation-resolved place representation known as directional histogram maps (DHMaps) through a single neural network. However, despite DHMaps' place representation effectiveness, their dimensionality makes them suboptimal for clustering and pose estimation between places. In response, we introduce two key innovations: first, we develop a merged projection technique that reduces DHMaps for dimensionality reduction while preserving their directionality and enabling efficient clustering and accurate cross-place pose estimation. Secondly, we integrate a correspondence learning module that refines the merged projection by minimizing the distance between corresponding DHMap pixels, thereby enhancing place accuracy. Our experiments demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed approach, achieving high precision in place estimation across a wide range of angles.

Long-range interactions, found in various physics contexts, are modeled by nonlocal theories, and this is particularly useful in describing the failure of materials with interatomic forces. This paper delicits a bond-based nonlocal theory of fluids, and the theory's aspects, including the connections to theoretical physics concepts and the mathematically equivalent theories, are explored in this review. This review focuses on bond-based nonlocal dynamics and examines the relevant mathematical properties, and mathematical equivalencies, of the underlying mathematical framework. Notably, the primary purpose of this work is to provide the necessary tools for the recent bond-based nonlocal theory of fluids to be rigorously analyzed and better understood.

Graphical Lasso algorithms are commonly used in analyzing complex systems that consist of multiple interconnected components. As research in this area advances, the need for a well-developed Python toolbox becomes apparent, offering efficient and easy-to-use Graphical Lasso calculations. This toolbox offers the following features: (1) it is compatible with Microsoft Windows, Mac OS X, and Unix/Linux systems; (2) it leverages the Parallel Graphical Lasso (GGLasso) algorithm for optimized calculations; and (3) it includes a user-friendly interface for interacting with the results. This toolbox is particularly useful in various applications, including neuroscience, machine learning, and machine diagnostics.

Numerous techniques exist to sample the configurational molecular space, with Langevin Dynamics (LD) standing out due to its straightforward physical and numerical implementation. Despite longstanding efforts to enhance the efficiency of Langevin Dynamics, the method often proves inadequate for accurately determining the free energy landscape, particularly when incorporating cofactors like electrostatic interactions. This research utilizes molecular dynamics to investigate the methanol dimer and trimer formation, as well as a lysozyme, to evaluate the performance of various configurational sampling methods based on the comparison of their respective structural and dynamical properties. Our findings suggest that conventional MD and the minimization of the mean force (MMF) methods yield the most reliable structural and dynamical properties for methanol dimers and trimers, while for lysozyme, a combination of configurational interaction (CI) and MMF (CMMF) yields the best outcomes. Although CI and CMMF demonstrate improved structural and dynamical properties over standard MD, they do not consistently match the performance of MD. As a result, we suggest adopting a hybrid strategy, utilizing CI or CMMF in conjunction with MMF to identify robust minima, then employing MD to evaluate the local dynamics surrounding these minima.

This research builds upon a previously developed general relativistic hydrodynamic model that accounts for the effects of black hole accretion on the surrounding matter, specifically the wave shadow phenomenon. The simulation framework was modified to incorporate this effect and was used to model the dynamics and light emitted during the fusion of two black holes with masses of 10 and 8 solar units. The simulation assumed the black holes were moving through a uniform matter environment and resulted in the formation of distinct features, such as the wave shadow, due to the accretion process. The size and location of the wave shadow varied depending on the flow of matter and was influenced by the formation of the accretion disk.

We investigate the long-term behavior of a specific type of beam, called the extended Euler-Bernoulli beam, when it's placed on a graph with one central point connected to multiple straight lines. This setup involves the beam undergoing transverse vibrations, and at the central point, there are connections to multiple straight lines that affect its movement. Mathematical models for this system were first developed in previous studies, and it's been shown that the system's vibrations gradually decrease over time, and certain frequencies don't appear in the system. In this research, we prove that a similar behavior occurs in a slightly modified version of the system, where the model accounts for the stiffness of the beam and the forces within it, and the model is improved to better reflect the underlying physics. This allows us to show that the vibrations decrease at an exponential rate over time.

Researchers in photoacoustic breast imaging commonly pair acoustic lenses with detection systems to increase the scanned region beyond the transducer's width without compromising spatial resolution or depth of focus. Unfortunately, this approach typically requires high-cost materials. A new class of polymer substances has been designed and analyzed to effectively function as acoustic lenses, yielding optimal results when matched with the frequencies used in clinical detectors, resulting in a 2.5 times increase in the covered area at no extra expense. The performance of these substances has been validated experimentally and their capabilities in enhancing PA breast imaging have been demonstrated numerically.

Community detection and node classification are pivotal problems within the fields of graph and network analysis that have significant real-world applications. Over the years, prominent methods have been developed to address these issues in various types of graphs and networks. Given the growing interest in researching and understanding the connections between different entities, multilayer networks have emerged as a vital area of study. To effectively analyze these complex structures, numerous frameworks have been proposed to model multilayer graphs and networks. In response to this development, we have introduced the concept of eigenvector prominence to characterize multilayer graphs and networks, which we've demonstrated provides a reliable descriptive framework for both community and node classification patterns. Theoretical analysis along with numerical experiments have revealed the RPI eigenvalues to be indicative of distinct high-value eigenvalues across different layers of these complex structures. Specifically, we've shown that the corresponding eigenvectors embody a localized form of the eigenvector centralization within each layer, leading to the identification of implicit substructures that encompass densely connected clusters of nodes and individual nodes with the highest overall central values, respectively. The eigenvector prominence method is objective, statistically quantifiable, and seamlessly integrates with existing multilayer frameworks such as the dependent node classification framework and the coherent community structure within multilayer networks found in existing literature. Moreover, we've employed this method to successfully identify implicit cluster structures in synthetic multilayer networks and accurately detect implicit prominent nodes in both single-layer and multilayer networks.

High-quality computational photography relies on removing various image degradations, particularly the unique, combined degradation that occurs in raw sensor data, which often includes demosaicing, deblurring, and denoising.  Traditionally, researchers have tackled this by processing the raw image through a sequence of individual degradation-removal steps, but the order and number of these steps can significantly impact the final result.  In an effort to enhance this approach, we trained a collaborative network that is capable of simultaneously performing demosaicing, deblurring, and de-noising, and discovered that this advanced model surpasses the sequential processing method.  When real-world noise and blur data are available for training, we discovered that incorporating them into a training regimen, rather than relying on synthetic simulations, yields more accurate results for the collaborative network.  To our knowledge, this is the initial study to apply collaborative learning to the demosaicing, deblurring, and de-noising processes.

This work extends previous findings from us in the journal Siam Journal on Applied Algebra and Computation (2019) by expanding the type of vectors considered in the phase space of $R$-Minkowski space to all of $\mathbb{R}^{n+1}$, rather than just the light cone. As a consequence, the Poisson bracket derived from the symplectic form on the $(n-1)$-sphere becomes representative of the Casimir function's role for the conformal group $SO(n+1,1)$. Furthermore, this bridge enables a connection to a form of the Connes-Landau-Polkingholke trace that aligns with the representation theory of the conformal group in R-Minkowski space, which we detail in the journal's final pages.

This paper introduces the Causal Exploration Toolbox (CEt), a comprehensive set of algorithms for exploring and inferring causality, with an emphasis on flexibility and adaptability. Built as an object-oriented framework in Python, CEt is designed to work with both observational and experimental data, addressing a wide range of statistical models. By leveraging the capabilities of the Statistical Learning Toolbox (SLT), users can evaluate the effectiveness of specific causal models and explore their underlying structures, with a view to establishing more accurate models of the world through a combination of human knowledge and data-driven exploration.

To understand how materials behave when exposed to corrosive substances, the liquid entry surface tension (LEST) phenomenon is a key factor.  Yading Chen and colleagues investigated how spheres interact with liquids under different levels of velocity, focusing on water, glycerol, and silicone oil.  By experimenting with velocities up to 4.3 meters per second, they observed that the spheres either become fully covered, partially covered, or not covered at all, depending on the liquid's thickness and the speed at which the sphere moves.  To analyze this, they created a new parameter incorporating the sphere's speed, the liquids' viscosity, and density.  Their research revealed that the spheres either get fully covered, partially covered, or not covered at all, based on the relationship between this parameter and specific numerical values for different liquids.  These findings provide valuable surface tension information and can be applied to designs in fields such as self-cleaning surfaces and inkjet printing.

In a generic Type IIB compactification, it is observed that, at the leading order in Kaluza-Klein powers of $M_{\rm Pl}$, the vacuum energy is minimized by a nonperturbative mechanism, such as an instanton or a $(0,2)$-deformation in the Calabi-Yau manifold, which breaks U(1) R-symmetry. This mechanism causes a set of nonperturbative gauge mediation superpotentials to take values that are on the order of $10^{-8} M_{\rm Pl}$. This EFT framework also enables an extension of the standard $\xi$-controlled, positive-definite, kinetic $\tau$-space via nonperturbative terms, such as $e^{-S}$ and $\xi$, such that, in order to achieve a vacuum energy of $10^{-8} M_{\rm Pl}^2$, the standard terms must be as small as $\xi \sim 10^{-20}$ and the potential must be balanced by an $e^{-S}$ term with an imaginary offset of $e^{i a_0 S}$. This universal behavior is shown to be consistent with perturbative constraints, and the unextended model is shown to possess $10^{10}$ distinct, discrete, and geometric vacua.

Secure Enclaves in modern CPUs are designed to handle sensitive tasks securely by isolating untrusted software and leveraging hardware features like memory encryption. Despite their effectiveness, recent research has revealed critical vulnerabilities in Secure Enclaves, enabling secret extraction from running applications or even enrolled keys in enclaves. To mitigate these vulnerabilities, researchers have introduced confidence levels to evaluate the reliability of enclave-based systems. In response, a novel architecture called Confidence-Minimizing Hardware (CMH) is proposed, which reduces the dependence of confidence on software and shifts the focus to universal, system-wide security assessments. CMH achieves this by providing complete control over a separate piece of hardware, isolated from the main system, through a custom interface. The CMH model demonstrates potential for enhancing applications that rely on secure enclaves, such as blockchain technology and identity management systems, in scenarios where enclave failures are not an option.

Multi-task Reinforcement Learning (ML) has proven effective in enhancing learning efficiency and robustness by integrating related tasks to support one another.
Nevertheless, real-world applications often face an unexpected surge in distributional changes or failures, resulting in data that misleads traditional Multi-task Learning (MTL) methods and leads to severe performance declines.
Furthermore, not all data contribute equally to the overall MTL system, presenting challenges in balancing the benefits of sharing among diverse tasks.
To address these issues, we introduce Resilient Policy Gradient (RPG), a unified and adaptive MTL framework that dynamically manages the level of task cooperation by learning from the data.
RPG incorporates the concept of plasticity to adaptively adjust the sharing of knowledge, enabling it to thrive on high-quality data and isolate its components in the face of data degradation.
By utilizing a mean-gradient model and a resilient policy gradient method, we are able to regulate the cooperative strategy and ensure the stability of the learning process.
Through extensive experiments in both continuous control and natural settings, our findings show that our proposed approach outperforms several state-of-the-art methods in terms of average and maximum performance, and also demonstrates superior resilience to sudden spikes in data quality.

In the context of the box game, we analyze a variant where "show" options are limited to one of the visible faces, and "bet" options are constrained to either zero or one. We identify the unique equilibrium in this restricted version, finding that it matches the optimal strategy only under specific circumstances. Notably, these circumstances can be significantly better achieved in the standard box game. Consequently, transferring principles of the optimal box game to the standard version of poker results in a notable decrease in profitability.

Our new material Cubanite (CuFe2S3) exhibits structural and magnetic order, with exceptions near the Fermi level in its electronic properties. Using X-ray techniques and theoretical calculations, we discovered that Cubanite's electronic structure changes under pressure, with distinct pressure ranges leading to different phases. These ranges include a metallic phase, two insulating phases with different orbital occupancies, and a second pressure range where insulating behavior reappears. Further study using DFT showed that Cubanite acts as a model for interacting electrons, with specific orbital occupancies in each insulating phase.

A compelling external-field-free dynamics, the dark Rabi oscillation, is achieved through a balance between the strong light-matter coupling and a sufficiently large effective mass of tightly confined whispering-gallery-mode (WGM) cavities and near-infrared frequency lasers. Using a generic three-level system with a dark laser excitation, it is possible to analytically determine the condition for WGM cavity radius, laser waist, and dark Rabi frequency. Numerical results show that the dark Rabi frequency increases as the WGM cavity radius and laser waist decrease, and this high-rate oscillation may allow for the development of swiftly operating, precisely controllable, and highly sensitive WGM cavity devices that operate without the need for external magnetic fields.

In two-dimensional non-symmorphic lattices, a variety of lattice structures can be found within each wallpaper category. Using a tight-binding model, we can see that the non-symmorphic nature of these space groups leads to non-trivial band crossings along high-symmetry lines or planes, forming a type of Dirac point/line. We non-symmorphic wall papers analyze the tight-binding parameters of the six non-symmorphic space groups in detail, focusing on four of them and discovering that in these cases, the Dirac lines/points can be located away from high-symmetry paths. This phenomenon provides new insight into the lattice design for achieving low-bandgap or gapless lattices. We also apply our theory to a CdTe-InSb ternary alloy with a non-symmorphic diamond structure, and experimental angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy confirms the existence of Dirac lines.

Quantum states that blend elements of classical and quantum mechanics extensively lie in the mid-range and exhibit unique entanglement characteristics. These complex superposition states are currently challenging to create, yet they are crucial for advancing fundamental quantum research and potential applications in quantum technology. Here, we present a quantum-optical catalysis scheme that can efficiently generate large-batch single-photon facilitated coherent states from a coherent state, by utilizing an on-off keying signal and non-classical entanglement. This process significantly increases the required transformation strength by up to two orders of magnitude compared to directly transforming classical coherent states into LSCS. By combining theoretical analysis with experimental data, we show that this proposed scheme is within reach of existing technology.

We've developed the NP formalism for the Einstein equations, especially in the context of the Maxwell equations, by utilizing the bivector NP four-forms. The BNPH framework has been introduced, which connects the BNP conditions to the Thorne rules in a way that relates isolated gravitational systems to the Todorov systems, where the Todorov conditions are a subset of the BNP conditions. The connection to the Todorov systems is further explained through the Todorov equations, a subset of the BNP conditions, and we obtained the Todorov equations from the Todorov normal form Todorov operator using de Rham's cohomology. The connection to the Todorov systems is also expressed in the NP spinor Todorov equations, and in the Todorov normal form Todorov T-operator, and the Todorov normal form T-operator leads to the T-operator equation, and T-operator is a (1,1)-tensor. The connection to the Todorov systems is also found in T-operator and it can be seen that T-operator is either the Todorov curvature or the sum of the Todorov curvature and the Todorov gauge field strength, and the elements of the Todorov curvature are the Todorov invariants. With the rapid pace of discoveries in polymer materials, identifying patterns and connections within this vast field has become challenging due to their complexity. This research presents a novel, data-driven methodology for analyzing the composition of bulk polymers using whole programming and linear regression, with the aim of deriving a predictive model that can estimate the polymer's properties based on its monomer components. This study initially demonstrates the effectiveness of this approach by applying it to a dataset consisting of 14 common polymers, with properties including heat deflection temperature, glass transition temperature, melting temperature, and tensile strength. Furthermore, the study explores potential extensions of this methodology to composite polymers, providing a foundation for future work in this area.

Music production often involves using "enhancement" tools to quickly enhance a track's overall sound without altering individual elements. This concept can be expanded to include real-time processing of live performances, providing listeners with an improved listening experience. However, few systems have been developed so far to achieve this. Our objective is to introduce a system capable of real-time transcription and generation of mixed audio, drawing from an overview of recent breakthroughs in sequence-to-sequence prediction models. Our system, based on end-to-end prediction, utilizes the FaFa architecture and is evaluated through a case study on predicting the mix of two people breathing during the COVID-19 pandemic. Findings indicate our model can accurately predict a mix of source signals, although results may vary with different genres and recording conditions. To facilitate the development of similar systems, we have made our data publicly available.

Esophageal tumors in society are considered highly malignant and are usually identified through endoscopic examination and X-ray imaging. Determining the size of these tumors is essential for accurate diagnosis, treatment planning, and monitoring of disease progression. With the rising prevalence of neoplasms, there's an urgent need for the development of efficient and precise methods for 3D segmentation of these tumors. In this study, we propose a novel deep learning-based framework, which encompasses data preprocessing, a customized 2D ground truth generation, and a uniquely designed deep learning architecture for accurate and efficient esophageal neoplasm segmentation. Our results show that the proposed method achieves outstanding performance metrics, including a Dice Similarity Coefficient (DSC) of 0.819, highlighting its efficiency and robustness in processing scans within a reasonable timeframe. With its user-friendly interface, our system provides users with a reliable and accessible method for neoplasms segmentation, thereby making advanced imaging analysis more accessible.

Determining subsurface properties from well log data is an essential part of geosteering.  Since the mid-2000s, statistical approaches like the Cramer and Bennett (2005) (C&B) framework have been widely employed to calculate confidence intervals around log property predictions.  Although several implementations of this model exist, a critical aspect that has been overlooked is how to effectively define the average and variability of the data from which properties are predicted.  This study aims to introduce a series of methods for making informed decisions on these inputs within the C&B framework, drawing on widely accepted statistical techniques for analyzing data.  By incorporating these strategies, the C&B framework can be applied to assess the uncertainty surrounding well log data, ultimately supporting more reliable geosteering decisions.  A successful implementation of this approach is demonstrated through a case study involving log analysis and well placement in a specific reservoir.

Name entity recognition has long been a key focus in natural language processing, now often treated as a distinct task. In this study, we shift the perspective by viewing names as indicators of overall document structure. Moving beyond traditional approaches that rely on linear pattern matching or simple cardiology, our proposed method, Nested NER, analyzes holistic document structures. By representing texts as parsed trees and leveraging the rich relational information, we achieve enhanced nested name entity detection results. Our experiments show that Nested NER outperforms state-of-the-art methods, particularly in detecting complex nested entities. We make Nested NER's source code and data accessible on GitHub for future reference.

We're examining the connection between rational and tropical hypersurfaces of a specific degree and genus on a cubic surface, establishing a correspondence to compute $\mathbb{A}^1$-genus and Euler characteristic for a set of bitangents. The bitangents to a specially chosen family of quartic surfaces in three-dimensional space are shown to be equivalent to the edges and vertices of a tropical object, denoted as a curve or graph. This equivalence allows us to calculate the Euler characteristic for a set of bitangents by analyzing the combinatorial structure of the tropical object. The bitangents are also found to have the same $\mathbb{A}^1$-count as certain plane curves through a process of deformation from a generic set of quartics. Furthermore, a method is developed to assign a sign to a real bitangent based on the real points of a corresponding edge in the tropical object, denated as a curve or graph. This method is shown to equal a portion of the Hodgson index of a specific set of bitangents when the sum is taken over all real bitangents.

This research focuses on locating target nodes within wireless sensor networks using a method known as multihop trilateration. The research takes into account the impact of radio communication on network performance, particularly from other technologies that operate on the same frequency. A research model is developed to determine the number of hops between nodes and the associated errors in distance calculations. The research also proposes an optimization procedure to minimize location errors by adjusting the reference nodes' distances based on the type of network disruption. The changes in network disruption are modeled and incorporated into the hop-based distance model. The research results, demonstrated through simulation, show the effectiveness of the proposed approach in improving location accuracy in 2D planes for different types of network disruption.

This paper introduces a new concept, the Code-Switching Barriers Index (CSBI), to address the challenges associated with code-switching in natural language processing, and offers guidance for developing robust code-switching-aware NLP systems for multilingual users.

The current method of evaluating automatic image description generation is primarily based on comparison with human-generated descriptions. The criteria for selecting human descriptions used for this purpose are not clearly defined. The proposed research aims to examine how having more reference descriptions per image impacts the results of this evaluation method. The proposed criteria are implemented and the outcomes demonstrate that utilizing an average of human-generated reference descriptions per image, rather than just one, can significantly improve the evaluation outcomes, thereby making the results less biased and providing a basis for a refined standard for evaluating automatic image descriptions.

The most stable form of Tantalum pentoxide ($Ta_2O_5$) remains a subject of debate, with multiple candidates identified but experimental verification difficult. In a recent study, we used first-principles calculations combined with stochastic simulations to explore potential low-symmetry phases and identify the most stable configuration of $Ta_2O_5$ in its base state. By applying a global minimization method within the Born-Oppenheimer approximation, we identified a candidate structure with the space group $P2_1$, which exhibited a significantly lower total energy than any previously reported $Ta_2O_5$ phases. This candidate structure was then subjected to further analysis, comparing its optical properties with experimental data, and was found to closely match the observed features, providing a plausible explanation for long-standing optical property measurements of $Ta_2O_5$ in its base state.

Geographic distribution of online communities is shifting from wide-ranging concentrations to localized groupings, a change that may be linked to the spread of misinformation. This paper examines how the geographic isolation of Reddit users affects the propagation of false information. Data from 1.3 million Reddit comments spanning six months was analyzed to map the geographic origin of each post and explore how geographic isolation relates to the spread of false information. Our findings suggest that geographic isolation can contribute to the spread of false information by hindering critical evaluation and reinforcing pre-existing beliefs. However, the effect of isolation on the spread of false information is not uniform across all subreddits. For some subreddits, isolated users are more likely to share false information due to the content's nature, but for others, they are less likely to do so. This research has implications for understanding the relationship between online community structure and the spread of false information, with potential applications for developing more effective interventions.

The fleeting nature of social media platforms makes them an appealing source of real-time information, yet the presence of unreliable misinformation poses a significant challenge. This problem is exacerbated by the difficulty in distinguishing between credible and dubious sources. Our research aims to tackle this challenge in the context of real-time news events. We present a novel approach that uses both content-based and source-reputation features to automatically classify news items as either credible or dubious. Our source-reputation model takes into account the historical track record of each source, reflecting their typical behavior in reporting events. Our system was rigorously tested on two distinct datasets, resulting in accurate classification of news items on events that unfold in real-time.

The integration of speech systems in robots is being enhanced through feedback from human trainers who teach robots tasks through demonstration and verbal explanation. Human instructors use speech to provide feedback on task success, difficulty, and difficulty, which can be used to improve how robots learn from human examples. A key aspect of this process involves identifying factors that influence human decision-making, which remains largely unexplored due to the difficulty of conducting experiments with physical tasks. To address this challenge, we conducted a series of tests in a laboratory setting where humans performed a task that is commonly used to study human decision-making, which involved making adjustments to a mechanical arm. Recordings of these tasks included data on the timing of human actions, the difficulty of the tasks, and their success rates. Our analysis revealed that human instructors' verbal explanations are linked to (1) the complexity of tasks, as indicated by the timing of their actions, (2) the difficulty of tasks, which can be measured by the effort required to perform them, and (3) task outcomes, which are influenced by the success or failure of the task. Based on these findings, we developed a preliminary system that allows a robot to learn from human trainers' verbal explanations, which demonstrated that it could accurately predict the performance of this system when applied to real-world scenarios.

The prevalence of random tree generation algorithms is limited by the availability of corresponding algorithms to create trees of the same node count but with different topological configurations. A new approach has been developed to create random trees based on a specified degree distribution, which in this case, is defined by the number of children for each node, and can be applied independently to each node based on pre-determined probability distributions.

The complexity of studying continuous systems in geometry and physics originates in the limitation of representing their equilibrium configurations using finite parameters. This issue is particularly apparent in the context of nonlinear theories involving associative structures, such as the Hamiltonian for the Euler-Arnold equation describing the motion of a rigid body with fluid contained within, expressed via the Fokker-Planchoirre (FP) operator. The complication arises from the fact that no standard associative structure can accurately capture the Hamiltonian flow of this equation, rendering it impossible to represent its equilibrium configurations using a finite set of parameters. This inaccuracy also extends to the widely used Kramers equation, which has been derived from the FP operator through standard procedures. As a consequence, neither the FP nor Kramers equation can be considered the geometric representation of the underlying Hamiltonian flow. Instead, we have formulated revised equations based on the linearization of the Euler-Arnold equation, whose solutions correspond to a subset of the original system's solutions, thus providing a more accurate derivation of a modified 'thermal' equation that supersedes the conventional Kramers equation.

The concept of a conversational interface, initially introduced by Weizenbaum in 1966, has a long history that has seen both significant advancements and limited practical applications due to the difficulties in assessing the quality of these systems. Evaluating a conversational agent's performance presents unique challenges, as human assessments can vary, and setting up controlled experiments to accurately measure its capabilities is a complex task. To address this, we have developed a comprehensive evaluation framework consisting of 60 controlled scenarios, designed to assess the quality of conversational agents in areas such as the systems capacity, adherence to factual accuracy, and adherence to social norms. This evaluation framework has been utilized to assess the quality of three distinct conversational agents, including the latest iteration of the NER-based Marybot, the BERT-drawn Maritalk, and a BERT-based fine-tuned system named BERT-bot, revealing that while earlier models often break down into conversational patterns and generate inaccurate responses, more recent models can engage in the conversation for a longer duration, albeit with limitations in controlling the length of the conversation.

The search for Planet X in the outer solar system has primarily been conducted by analyzing the orbital characteristics of distant Kuiper Belt Objects, though previous studies have suggested a planet may already be evident in the gravitational effects on the inner solar system's known planets and moons. Using full Newtonian simulations, we compared the observed and predicted paths of the six innermost planets over several decades, discovering a noticeable discrepancy that couldn't be accounted for by relativistic corrections. Interestingly, this discrepancy follows a very specific, almost circular pattern in the sky, with its center located near the celestial south pole. When we simulated the removal of Planet X from our simulations, the resulting paths showed the same South-situatd pattern, indicating that Planet X's mass, size, and position could in fact be determined from the data. Based on this, we estimate that Planet X has a mass between 0.5 to 4.5 times that of Earth, with its center likely somewhere near the horizon in the constellation of Corona Australis. Furthermore, this discovery has significant implications for the historical record, with evidence of Planet X's gravitational influence potentially detectable in the paths of the innermost moons since as far back as 1990.

Previous research into Multilingual Neural Machine Translation (MNMT) relied on
monolingual translation models trained in separate stages, or utilized a single
neural machine translation (NMT) model for all language pairs. In contrast, our
proposed approach, called Multi-Translation Archive (MTA), combines the strengths
of both methods. MTA utilizes a monolingual translation archive to enrich the
translation space for each target language, allowing for a significantly reduced
archive size. Notably, experiments with the MTA approach have achieved remarkable
results, surpassing the MNMT and single NMT baselines by a substantial margin.
For instance, it has achieved a reduction in Word Error Rate (WER) of 10.12 words
per sentence on the De-En task, a 5.25-point improvement in F1 score on the Zs-En
task, as well as an 8.25-word reduction in WER on the En-Zs task.

We update the predictions of Conformal Cyclic Cosmology (CCC) concerning the Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB), specifically the location and size of the HB spots, which could help distinguish CCC from the Standard Model of Cosmology ($\Lambda$CDM). The position of these spots is expected to follow the distribution of hot and cold anomalies in the CMB, but current data show significant discrepancies. The predicted spot sizes in the CCB model are larger than those typically found in the CMB. The analysis takes into account the Hubble tension, which arises from the difficulty in reconciling the measured expansion rate of the universe with the value derived from the early universe's characteristics. The study also considers the possibility of placing constraints on the pre-big bang parameters based on the location of these HBs. The analysis uses a Bayesian framework to map the characteristics of the pre-big bang universe to the HBS on the CMB sky. The analysis focuses on the location and size of the HBS, as well as their distribution, which is expected to follow the distribution of clusters in the pre-big bang universe. The study finds that the predicted HBS will appear as small, low-variance spots in the CMB, which could be used to further test the CCC model. The analysis finds that the predicted HBS will appear as a sparse pattern of spots in the CMB, which is consistent with the observed lack of significant temperature fluctuations in the CMB. This paper proposes a novel approach called Prototype Learning with Relaxed Constraints (PLRC) to improve the ability to recognize objects from a new class using only a few samples. In contrast to traditional methods, which require a large number of training samples, our method allows the use of a class from only a single sample. To accomplish this, we designed a novel way to generalize the KLD minimization objective, which is typically used in the one-class case, in order to minimize the distance between a class prototype and its corresponding distribution. The results of our experiments on multiple datasets, including a large-scale evaluation on ILSVR, demonstrate the superiority of PLRC over existing methods. Source code for the method is available online.

Cross-domain recommendation systems have gained significant attention for enhancing sparsely-rated users' recommendation accuracy. However, most existing methods focus on handling single sparse-domain recommendations, neglecting users with multiple sparse-rated domains. These methods also struggle to effectively capture users' hidden preferences across different domains. To address these challenges, we propose a novel single sparse-domain cooperative recommendation framework called Improved Thorough Aspect Preference Learning. This framework involves two key cooperative strategies: (i) enhancing users' latent preferences through multi-aspects analysis and (ii) aligning users with consistent interests through adaptive similarity learning. Experimental results demonstrate that our method outperforms current recommendation approaches, yielding substantial improvements in recommendation performance and achieving over 10% gain in F-measure.

Organic molecules often adopt complex, asymmetrical structures, which can be challenging to model geometrically and chemically. This work introduces a comprehensive, parametric framework for defining planar or 3D organic Conics, applicable to up to 20 atoms. The framework facilitates the automated resolution of optimization problems involving constrained organic molecules in three dimensions. A key feature of this framework is its ability to convert chemically and geometrically constrained molecules into a format that can be efficiently solved, with the aim of finding stable molecular configurations. The framework is accompanied by a high-level programming language, Hypatia.jl, which provides pre-built chemical building blocks and enables the description of molecules in a concise and intuitive manner. The framework is demonstrated its ability to resolve organic molecules in planar or 3D space, with up to 19 atoms, through a series of tests that include benzene, toluene, toluene-dimer, and toluene-trimer. The framework is set to be a valuable tool for a wide range of applications, including theoretical chemistry and materials science, by enabling the efficient design and modeling of molecules and materials.

Multiple magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) quality assessment tools are essential for accurately identifying and correcting anomalies in MRI images, a process that is labor-intensive and costly. To address this, a single neural network was developed with the capability to generalize across various MRI quality assurance tasks, potentially limiting the need for retraining when dealing with different imaging conditions. Building on previous research, a new dataset was created consisting of over 1,000 three-dimensional brain MRI images covering multiple quality categories. A convolutional neural network was trained using this extensive dataset with the goal of demonstrating multi-task quality evaluation. However, despite notable improvements compared to evaluating each quality assurance task separately, a significant issue of poor generalization was found. Analysis revealed that certain difficult-to-generalize patterns existed within a specific dataset configuration, leading to a conclusion that further study is required to understand and overcome these limitations. To facilitate such research, a comprehensive guide was created to systematically examine dataset characteristics and their impact on generalization capabilities.

Enter persistent memory, a novel class of computer memory, bridging the gap between volatile and non-persistent memory types. The Optane DC Persistent Storage Module, or DC PM, is an enterprise data center solution built on the Optane DC memory technology, which automatically preserves data across system rebocks through persistent extensions of languages like C++ and Java. Based on a custom file system called DCFS, our research focuses on assessing the performance of DC PM based storage applications by exploring various file system configurations, data writing strategies, and concurrency control methods. Our findings reveal that the optimal configuration of DCFS, combining write batching, B+ tree indexing, and list locking, yields a performance boost of up to 27x for random random access operations compared to its unoptimized form. Notably, our findings are language-agnostic and can be applied to a wide range of applications, from key-value stores to machine learning models. The source code for DCFS is publicly available on GitHub under the Apache License 2.0.

In planning for multiple agents, a key challenge is meeting utilization, which aims to maximize the number of agents that can collaborate with each other. A common way to represent this collaboration is using a graph, but the size of which can rapidly grow, hindering traditional methods. To address this issue, we propose a new approach that considers the number of edges connected to each node, incentivizing agents to work with more teammates. Our solution uses a time-based model that represents the work being done, defined by a set of tasks and individual agent actions. Through a unique framework, we can efficiently execute this plan even with a limited number of agents. Our approach also features a decentralized system that processes each decision independently, allowing it to scale to large problems. Experimental results show the effectiveness of this method in various scenarios, including one with ten agents that has already been simulated.

This research examines the structural, electronic and magnetic properties of rare-earth sesquiferrostanates GdSn3 and CmSn3, and a series of CsSn3 alloys using first-principles calculations. We find that all these materials adopt the AuCu3 crystallographic structure (F43m). Our results show that CmSn3 has a localized 5d electron configuration, in contrast GdSn3 displays both localized 4f and 4d electron characteristics. Notably, CmSn3 shows higher magnetic moments (4.5 $\mu_B$) compared to GdSn which exhibits magnetic moments of 3.5 $\mu_B$. Our calculations further reveal that the band gaps of GdSn3 and CmSn3 are indirect, direct, and 0.48 eV, respectively. Furthermore, our findings suggest that the formation of Gd-Cm sesquiferrostanates is feasible under ambient conditions.

For over 40 years, observations of the visible universe have shown that normal, or "baryonic" matter accounts for only a small fraction of the total mass-energy content of the cosmos. This discrepancy has motivated a search for "dark baryons" – entire galaxies made up of hidden, free-floating atomic nuclei and clouds of hydrogen. In this work, we forecast potential tests for such hidden baryonic matter using upcoming or recently released data sets from multiple astronomical fields. These include visible light, X-rays, radio astronomy, gamma rays, and data from gravitational lensing and particle colliders. If such matter exists and makes up a significant portion of dark matter, it should be detectable through multiple methods, or at least in multiple wavelength ranges or data sets. Thus, the existence of such "dark baryonic" matter is subject to scrutiny from several scientific communities simultaneously.

The fundamental theorem of Coxeter group type B has a concise quantitative formulation, which we aim to generalize to the B-type parabolic subgroups of a Coxeter group. We achieve this generalization through the use of parabolic quotients and provide the corresponding expression for crystal bases of various convex polytopes, including the permutahedron, cyclohedron, and truncated cube.

Using an estimate for the matter power spectrum that accounts for lensing effects without the need to solve the geodesic equations, we have assessed the impact of cosmic shear on the observed flux of Type Ia supernovae. By comparing various methods of accounting for this effect, including neglecting it, including only diagonal effects, or including the full matrix, we found that the difference in results corresponds to approximately 0.01 sigma. This indicates that the Pantheon dataset is not significantly affected by lensing effects. As such, our study provides valuable insights for upcoming surveys like DESI and Euclid, which will produce significantly larger datasets. By analyzing the superimposed effects of shear and other factors that influence flux measurements, our study found that the residuals in the data are consistent with expectations, within 1 sigma. To further illustrate our findings, we have created a Python tool that can be used to apply lensing corrections to any dataset of Type Ia supernovae.

In this research, we analyze and simulate two types of cross-shaped waveguide junctions made from silicon-on-dielectric (SOD) material. Specifically, we investigate a dielectric SOD and a metallic SOD with an added thin gold layer. Through finite-difference time-domain (FDTD) and mode-matching methods, we determine the dielectric characteristics of these structures and their corresponding beta values. Our findings from these two approaches are in agreement. Notably, the mode-matching method provides more precise results for the metallic SOD structure. We also explore how various design parameters, including arm width and bending angles, influence the dielectric properties of these structures, and our results can be used to create lookup tables for photonic circuit designers using SOD technology.

These methods are demonstrated through actual MRI images and their respective
protocols are provided for potential replication. Categorizing these techniques
into physics-based and unrelated groups allows for a clearer understanding of their
respective impacts on the accuracy of deep learning models used for image analysis.

Wireless sensor networks (WSNs) have been instrumental in providing data collection and monitoring capabilities for various applications. Despite their widespread use, certain functions of the network remain underdeveloped, particularly those related to information aggregation. A novel approach, the Greedy on-demand Gather approach, addresses this by allowing for efficient data transmission and a reduced energy consumption through careful planning of the network's hierarchy and connectivity. A corresponding algorithm, H-BIGLE, employs a combination of techniques to organize the network into hierarchical levels and estimate the integrity of connections between sensors and the base station, ensuring reliable data transmission. Simulation results show that H-BIGLE is effective in creating the network hierarchy proposed, resulting in more energy-efficient operations and successful level transitions for a majority of sensors.

This paper presents an advanced context-aware system for identifying objects in three-dimensional space, particularly for detecting scenarios like obstacles, pedestrians, and road signs. The context is established by analyzing the spatial relationships and connectivity of objects in the scene. To validate the effectiveness of this context in three-dimensional space, we collected and processed LiDAR data from a real-world environment, creating a comprehensive 3D scene with associated 2D and 7D scene contexts. The context is also explored from the perspectives of local and global connectivity, as well as reachability. We designed a context-aware detector that leverages these hierarchical scene contexts to enhance the accuracy of three-dimensional space object detection. Our context-aware model outperformed traditional two-stage and single-stage detectors in this domain.

The prescribed mathematical problem involves an element $u\in H^1(\mathbb{R}^N)$ which satisfies the equation where $\lambda$ is a non-negative real parameter, $y$ denotes the identity function on $\mathbb{R}$, and $e^{\beta u}$, $\frac{\gamma}{|x|^{(N-2)/2}}e^{\gamma u}$, and $\frac{\delta}{|x|^{(N-2)/2}}e^{\delta u}$ are integrable with respect to $dx$ and $d\mu$, respectively. Its behavior is examined within the framework of whole space $\mathbb{R}^N$ for dimension three or greater, involving the combination of Kirchhoff type framework, Lamberto-Egbert-Moser growth, and singular Trudinger-Moser growth. Our main finding is that for sufficiently large $\max\{\beta,\gamma,\delta\}$, the prescribed mathematical problem has at least one infinite sequence of elements that converge weakly, which constitutes a novel result in the field.

The sum of $n$ independent binary random variables $X_i$, where $P(X_i=1)=p_i$ and $p_i+p_j\le 1$ for any $i\ne j$, has a concentration inequality derived in this work. The given upper bound for the conditional probability $P(\sum_{i=1}^n X_i - E[\sum_{i=1}^n X_i]\ge t)$ is $\exp\left(-\frac{t^2}{2\sum_{i=1}^n p_i(1-p_i) + t\max_{1\le i\le n}\{p_i(1-p_i)\}}\right)$. Notably, when $n$ is an odd integer, the scenario where $p_i=1/(n+1)$ for all $i$ maximizes this upper bound, leading to the comparison with the concentration inequality for independent binary random variables from Chebyshev's inequality.

Building upon previous work by Rubin and Schoof who expanded Fontaine-Messing theory to power series algebras, we further generalize this framework. This extension allows for the application of the Fontaine-Messing framework in the context of abelian varieties without needing the initial restriction that their Newton polygons must be strict.

We derive a new geometric formula linking the rate at which a rotating cylindrical shell emits de Sitter radiation to the surface area of a de Sitter body defined by that same shell. This relationship holds for any de Sitter object, including those made of microscopic particles, as long as they rotate while emitting radiation in equilibrium. It effectively bridges the surface area concept from de Sitter quantum electrodynamics with a more fundamental rate of change in area. It also indicates that Eddington's principle of number, which underlies the microcanonical de Sitter atmosphere, arises from non-gravitational electromagnetic interactions occurring on the cylindrical horizon.
