This research focuses on analyzing the effect of changing loss functions in the context of deep learning-based classification models. We examined a range of functions with common properties in a well-established benchmark dataset. Our findings reveal that, for models with many parameters, the loss function's alteration significantly influences the model's output. This outcome highlights the necessity of further research into loss function design with a view to enhancing model performance.

A stabilization technique for the Navier-Stokes equations is developed using a boundary feedback controller at an angle relative to the domain's boundaries. The study employs the backstepping methodology to achieve asymptotic stability through a PDE-PDE system. Key properties of the controlled system are established, and sufficient conditions for stability are derived. The resulting controller demonstrates robustness to certain external disturbances. Finally, a boundary observability technique ensures the feasibility of the control scheme.

This research utilizes a well-established thermodynamic framework to model the coupled mechanical and thermal behavior of semocrystalline polymers during their melting and crystallization processes. The primary cause of crystallization in these materials, however, is the application of mechanical loads. The simulation employs the Darcy-Panjer approach, which addresses the mechanical and thermal interactions within the model. The results indicate that, for nearly incompressible materials like polymers, an alternative model reduction can effectively capture the mechanical and thermal processes induced by load application. The success of the developed simulation was validated through numerical tests, including the development of a monolithic solution method utilizing the generalized minimal residual algorithm. The final model's capabilities were fully demonstrated in the context of predicting microstructure formation in high-density polyethylene loadings.

To understand the dynamic properties of triplet Cooper pairs in a nematic superconductor, we have performed a systematic analysis of the Pippard superconducting response within the framework of mean-field theory. Our findings reveal that the symmetry of the superconducting state influences the London penetration depth and the nuclear scattering mean free path, with specific anisotropy in the superconducting gap enabling the observation of London oscillations under a rotating magnetic field. Notably, we found that the London penetration depth exhibits two distinct components, with one arising from Pauli paramagnetism and the other from the Zeeman effect. As a result, the dominant cause of the shift in the London oscillation period is the Zeeman effect, with the penetration depth remaining largely unaffected by the material's anisotropy due to Pauli paramagnetism.

Next-generation robotics will be heavily reliant on real and virtual training methods that utilize constructive digital feedback from simulations or virtual environments. These methods will allow for the development of complex behaviors in a controlled setting before being transferred to a physical robot. Current frameworks for feedback-based learning in software are being outpaced by the growing demands of advanced robotics applications, leading to a critical need for innovation in this field. In this paper, I present a unified perspective on feedback-based machine learning techniques for software systems and outline a general strategy for designing learning algorithms that utilize constructive digital feedback. This framework has potential applications in a wide range of robotics fields, and to demonstrate the power of these methods, the paper includes several case studies that explore the application of this framework to locomotion, manipulation, and scene understanding.

Difference Convolutional Markov Coded Detection, an non-coherent detection technique, was previously known to suffer from differential delay degradation caused by filtering. A corresponding delay enhancement differential DCCM detection technique is introduced, utilizing a 2x delay difference filter to fully compensate for degradation, resulting in equalized performance comparable to standard differential CPM detection. A significant finding reveals that for binary CPM, the conventional differential detection method is essentially a delayed version of the enhanced method, demonstrating their equivalence.

Researchers have developed statistical models to determine the likelihood of merging black holes with the cosmos' expanding structure, but these models lack consideration for the likelihood of such events actually occurring. To comprehend multi-messenger astronomy's potential, researchers must also identify the conditions under which these mergers can be detected. This research develops the necessary frameworks to detect core-collapse phenomena in supernovae and determines the conditions under which the product of the merger's density and the detection probability can be used to create realistic models for gravitational-wave and electromagnetic-wave observations. This research demonstrates the value of utilizing the concept of "source production rate" in determining the parameters of the model for the general population of such events, and it argues that incorporating information from the detection of core-collapse in supernovae is crucial for creating realistic models that accurately reflect the parameters of black hole-neutron star mergers, and it establishes the foundational concepts and methods for implementing this detection concept using the example of the lower limit of the neutron star mass distribution.

Building on previous research into the quantum potential concept, a new model has been developed to quantify the compressibility of thermal vacuum. The model demonstrates that the quantum potential density of this vacuum varies with temperature and exhibits thermal properties, allowing the vacuum's compressibility to change in response to thermal fluctuations. A further analysis has been introduced to study the thermal variation of these quantities, along with a discussion on the significance of finding that the quantum potential density of the vacuum remains finite even at very low temperatures, specifically as they approach absolute zero.

The Disentangled Image Generation project aims to simultaneously simulate and real-world rain effects on real images with accurate timing.  Using MSRA Rain Images as input, our model is evaluated based on whether the simulated rain in images matches the actual rain seen in the images.  Our Disentangled Image Transformation Network learns two separate transformations - one for adding rain and another for removing it - by mapping images to a latent space that's designed to always have the rain effect.  Features from images that aren't related to rain are preserved during this process.  A multi-task learning approach is used to give the network the ability to perform both rain simulations and eliminations well.  Our method is simple and effective, showing great results when evaluated with metrics like L1, L2, PSNR, and SSIM scores.

One common approach to solving the cluster control problem involves leveraging the cluster names as a reward signal, but this method can be time-consuming and subjective. To address these issues, we propose a more efficient method called Visually Supported Cluster Ranking (VSUR), where we engage human users in ranking the name-ordering of a selected subset of clusters and present them with a heat map that highlights the potential impact on final performance. Our approach allows human users to efficiently identify the optimal cluster name-ordering with minimal comparisons, resulting in an average of 5.3 times fewer comparisons needed than traditional methods and 1.4 times fewer comparisons needed than other efficient algorithms when achieving equivalent performance levels.

The research into the continuum issue within the set theory community has been significantly impacted by the adoption of various foundational frameworks, including the frameworks that influence theoretical outcomes. A continuum issue can present different aspects depending on its examination within a specific framework, and consequently, the concept of "completing" such issues becomes highly framework-specific. This paper delves into the concept of "completing" such issues within distinct frameworks and explores how the choice of framework can affect the perception of the continuum issue, utilizing the notion of "companion" frameworks to articulate these ideas. Furthermore, it examines the concept of the "price" of a completed such issue in relation to its companion framework. As an illustrative example, this paper discusses the result of Woodin on the ideal property of a companion framework and its implications on the arithmetic of a certain cardinal in the context of his work on the continuum issue.

On an n-dimensional Euclidean space, we establish a connection between the Q-curvature integral vanishing and the Weyl curvature tensor norm's behavior near the point at infinity, specifically when Q-integrable w.r.t Lebesgue measure dxdydz implies a Q-negligible Weyl curvature tensor norm at infinity in a confined area. Our findings are applicable to star-shaped confined areas and certain non-star-shaped confined areas.

Our research expands the traditional Five Factor Framework by incorporating character traits and linking it to assessments of substance use risks for adolescents. Based on this modified framework, we created a measurement tool and applied it to a sample of 1454 middle school students in southern China. Using confirmatory factor analysis, we validated the instrument and examined its ability to predict drug use risk through hierarchical regression analysis. The results show that after accounting for demographic factors, 27.1% of the variability in drug use risk can be explained by character and the five major personality traits. Specifically, honesty, self-discipline, and agreeableness have a direct, positive impact on drug use risk, while openness and neuroticism have indirect effects, working through the mediating role of the other three traits. Our valid character assessment tool and the underlying five-factor model can be effectively used to evaluate drug use risk in adolescent populations.

If-Then inference has historically been a challenging area for knowledge-based systems, as they have to infer missing parts of the rule structure that are not explicitly stated in the Pandas API knowledge base. To address this issue, we present a pre-built atlas of 108 rules involving up to 5-arg Pandas operations, covering the knowledge gap. Each rule in our atlas represents a logical connection between 4 entities, with the missing fifth entity being inferable from the other three. To make the atlas more usable, it is formatted as an SQL table and made searchable via the SQL-JDBC API. This format enables us to evaluate its performance through 10 carefully designed end-to-end benchmarks. Our findings show that our new atlas can significantly enhance the per-task and overall performance by a factor of 1.5X to 2.5X compared to the baseline, particularly when there is a high degree of missing information in the queries.

This paper presents NISQ-HHL, a new short-term neural network inspired by the HHL algorithm, designed to solve systems of linear equations. Initially applied to solving the Schrödinger equation for the hydrogen atom's ground state, our approach demonstrates superior performance to NISQ-GD, a recent benchmark method. For NIGQ-HHL to function, our proposal involves two simplified versions: one that approximates the inverse operation with a series of Fourier transforms, and another that employs the Chebyshev approximation, requiring only a rotation angle in each layer. Our research includes a new short-term circuit for the phase function, enabling our method to directly optimize the parameters within the system's evolution, thus bypassing the need for the variational approach, as shown in our results on the Portfolio Allocation Problem, where our method yields consistently better portfolio returns compared to VQ-HHL and NIGQ-HHL baselines.

The abundance of paired text-speech data on the internet presents a significant opportunity to train high-quality speech recognition models. Leveraging this resource, a novel approach called Bidirectional Speech-Text Focus (BiSTF) has been developed, which trains both speech and text models concurrently. In contrast to the traditional method of training both models independently, BiSTF focuses on training the speech model using text data and vice versa, effectively doubling the available training resources. To prevent the models from copying each other's predictions, a contrastive loss function is introduced. Experimental results demonstrate that incorporating text data significantly boosts performance on low-resource speech recognition tasks and that BiSTF achieves state-of-the-art results in low-resource scenarios. Furthermore, our method yields impressive outcomes in end-to-end models.

This research investigates the median cross-sectional width of simple closed curves in the plane. Unlike previous studies focusing on extremal properties, this work targets non-rigidity by examining the distribution of this parameter. The study also compares the distribution of median cross-sectional lengths between random curves and straight lines. A key contribution is the development of an efficient algorithm to calculate the distribution of these lengths, which is applied to a size-biased model of triangle-free chords within convex polygons.
For a uniformly selected parking function from the set {1, 2,..., n}^m, we examine the asymptotic expected values of its largest initial sequences.

investigators have long studied the electrical properties of thin superconducting films and islands, which exhibit zero resistance in certain circumstances and resistance up to e/Rh in others. 
 The mechanism behind this behavior has been extensively studied, with a recent study proposing that coherent quantum phase-jumps of a single charge carrier cause this resistance. 
 The new research aims to clarify the underlying mechanism in narrow superconducting nanowires, which have not been previously addressed. 
 Scientists have now performed experiments in highly doped niobium nitride nanowires, which have a very short coherence length and an energy gap that is comparable to the critical photon energy. 
 The experiments revealed an oscillatory pattern in the resistance of gate-tuned Josephson junctions in narrow nanowires, indicating that the previously proposed mechanism of Coulomb blockade does not apply in this context. 
 The scientists have now established a new model that incorporates large quantum fluctuations of the Josephson mode in a single-junction system to explain the observed behavior in these nanowires.

The initial free-floating T-dwarf, GJ 229B, is a type of brown dwarf that is significantly smaller and less luminous than its predecessor GJ 229A, a main-sequence star. Despite being discovered in 1995 through its stellar parent, GJ 229A, it is now known to have a different orbital path around GJ 229A, with evidence pointing to it being detected via its stellar parent's spectrum for the first 20 years after its discovery. By analyzing the spectrum of GJ 229B using the APOLLO code, a Bayesian method, the atmospheric composition of the object has been determined, along with estimates for its surface temperature, mass, and age. By comparing the results of this analysis to existing literature, the findings of the study are consistent with previous research, but with greater precision due to a more rigorous statistical approach. Additionally, by simulating different atmospheric compositions, the research group is planning to refine its analysis in the future. GJ 229B is a key object of study for exoplanets, as its spectrum is similar to that of some gas giants, and it is essential for validating detection methods that rely on comparing direct imaging spectra to atmospheric models.

By adapting the jet quenching parameter concept to its relativistic version, a consistent within-medium parameter is established, which characterizes the profound inelastic scattering experienced by high-energy partons due to interactions with the quark-gluon fluid.

Predicting changes in a scene based on a sequence of videos is a challenging task due to the complex relationship between an image's content and how it changes over time. To address this, our method converts the visual information in video frames into a sequence of embeddings that capture the key features of each image, effectively decoupling the content from the temporal dynamics. By utilizing a dual neural network structure, this sequence of embeddings is then used to generate and outline local predictions for object positions, sizes, and other relevant details in a subsequent video sequence. Notable object relationships are learned through a similarity matrix, which is used to generate an descriptive scene narrative that aids in making accurate whole-image predictions. Experiments on the challenging Youtube-TomsTheKitchen dataset reveal a significant improvement in prediction performance compared to existing methods, with our model reducing error rates by at least 10%.

Valence forces beyond the intra-site type, specifically inter-site interactions between adjacent d-orbitals, are vital for comprehending the behavior of transition metals within various materials. Although these inter-orbital interactions are crucial, current generative methods like density functional theory already take into consideration them to some extent, leaving the need for explicit, user-defined inter-orbital interactions in material modeling somewhat unclear. Here, using a combination of experiments and high-precision measurements on cuprate insulators, we provide direct, definitive evidence that these inter-orbital interactions are substantially significant, accounting for as much as 20% to 30% of the intra-site Coulomb interaction, a critical factor in the development of superconductivity. Our empirical evidence suggests that the necessary inter-orbital interactions should be directly incorporated into the density functional theory for the precise and reliable prediction of material properties.

The Ω-baryon, which contains sss quarks and has never been seen before, serves as a key focus in our study. Using the QCD sum rule method, we calculated various states of hadrons with different spin-parity combinations (J P) while varying the sss quark's mass. Our results indicate that the theoretical mass of the ground state Ω-baryon matches the experimental value very closely. Additionally, we found that the spectral density function is highly sensitive to the sss quark mass within the sub-threshold range. Our theoretical predictions for excited states of hadrons, such as 3/2 P, 5/2 S, 3/2 D, 5/2 D, and 7/2 S, also provide a consistent understanding of the observed resonances.

In forecast models for infectious diseases, incorporating personal interaction data can significantly improve accuracy. However, the benefit of incorporating social connectivity details varies greatly depending on the setting and the underlying transmission dynamics, presenting a challenge due to the lack of social connectivity details in available infection datasets. This study presents an alternative approach that derives exposure statistics from a social mixing matrix, using a case study of influenza among bus riders in the United States. The study shows that even data from highly mixed settings yields exposure history that can be derived from the social mixing matrix alone, using data on the number of people, volume of interactions, and age of participants. The derived exposure history on urban buses proves to be highly beneficial in forecast models, resulting in more accurate exposure predictions and significantly reduced exposure history exposure bias. The study also demonstrates that the derived exposure history on urban buses can be applied to public health initiatives, such as promoting mask-wearing, to makeexposure history more manageable and reduce exposure bias significantly. The study's findings suggest that the proposed approach can be applied to other highly mixed settings, providing valuable insights into the value of social connectivity details in infectious disease forecast models.

Quantum electrodynamics predicts a series of previously undetected effects resulting from photon interactions with the quantum vacuum, specifically the stochastic splitting of a photon's trajectory and the creation of color separation during the photon's propagation through flat space. To facilitate the development of direct photon trajectory and color separation observation, as well as the design of suitable detection systems, a theoretical analysis has been conducted to determine the optimal conditions for these experiments and identify the most effective detection methods for observing quantum vacuum diffraction and double refraction phenomena. This analysis covers both idealized theoretical scenarios and practical, experimentally feasible setups, focusing on the minimum conditions required to detect quantum vacuum diffraction and double refraction, as well as the specific requirements for detection methods based on various experimental configurations.
The algorithm devised by J. M. Eisenlohr and S. L. Farris is adapted to facilitate the systematic calculation of properties for fully transitive polyhedra defined by their vertex figure data.

A. Hoshiere's rejection of Daniel Simmons' "Unrepeatable Encryption" algorithm is based on a perceived reiteration of the key in each iteration of an XOR loop, which Hoshiere contends prevents the scheme from passing a basic confidentiality test. Nonetheless, as advocated by Daniel Simmons in his response, no such excessive key replication occurs, and 40 iterations are more than adequate for securing a 40-bit key against a brute force attack's threat. Nonetheless, it should be noted that the proposed system's security solely relies on the length and complexity of the passphrase, not the particular form of the algorithm, which may or may not be considered a reiteration of the argument made by A. Hoshiere.

This research paper presents a verification method for device-to-device (D2D) authentication in noisy environments. Unlike traditional methods, it avoids relying on pre-shared keys, instead utilizing a statistical test to determine authenticity based on observed signals. The proposed method's performance is evaluated analytically for noisy conditions, and results show that it can accurately authenticate devices when signal-to-noise ratios are below 20dB. However, to prevent fraudulent devices from deceiving the system through statistical test manipulation, a method of adaptive verification is introduced.

We calculate the electrical properties of twisted transition metal dichalcogenides along specific crystal directions, and find that surface plasmons can be significantly reduced in wavelength due to long-range Coulomb interactions. This effect occurs in both types of twisted structures, where the twist angle determines the plasmon behavior. Notably, at "magic angles," the surface plasmons exhibit unique patterns, allowing for the identification of different modes through the thickness of the device, and revealing the existence of bulk and boundary-bound plasmons. These findings may help guide the design of twisted TMDs for surface plasmonics applications.

This research extends the properties of a gradient Ricci soliton on a Sasakian manifold. We have demonstrated that a conformal Ricci soliton can be classified as a conformal harmonic Ricci soliton when its potential vector field is a Killing potential vector field. Additionally, we have established that a gradient Ricci soliton is equivalent to a conformal harmonic Ricci soliton when its potential vector field is a Killing potential vector field. We have also found that a conformal Ricci soliton holds true when its scalar curvature is not constant, and the potential vector field is a closed 1-form. It can also be shown that a conformal Ricci soliton is equivalent to a non-uniform expanding gradient Ricci soliton under specific conditions.

This report provides the resourced wind and magnetosphere data for various celestial entities, encompassing protostars, T Tauri and Herbig Be stars, as well as our solar system's planets and moons. It utilizes specialized indicators to describe these phenomena. A key distinction is drawn between celestial bodies with active magnetic fields, whose winds are regulated by these fields, and those with inert magnetic fields, where thermal controls dictate these wind characteristics. This differentiation is particularly evident in Jovian planets, but also appears in terrestrial bodies like Venus and Mercury. Venus exhibits no magnetosphere due to its field's inability to counter the solar wind's dynamic pressure, whereas Mercury has a substantial one.

Spin-orbit proximity effects in heavy elements like Bismuth require an in-depth understanding, which could lead to improved performance in spintronic devices involving adjacent materials. A key question arises about the origin of these complex effects: do they result directly from a material's intrinsic properties or indirectly through its lighter adjacent elements? Specifically, the spin-Hall effect in Bismuth cobalt multilayers, particularly in thin films with very thin Bismuth layers, exhibits an unusually high intensity that may have significant implications for understanding these effects. The unusual behavior at the boundary of these films cannot be accounted for by conventional bulk models, suggesting a possible link to the scattering of electrons and their spin-related components. By manipulating the boundary conditions and electron scattering types, it becomes possible to switch the direction of the observed effects, offering a new perspective on the role of Bismuth in this context.

A modified fractional Schrödinger equation is presented for a modified Mie-type potential in higher dimensions using the Jumarie type fractional derivative.  Employing a suitable factorization technique, we successfully obtained an invariant scheme for this modified potential.  Additionally, we derived specific conditions, a supersymmetric partner potential, and a family of time-independent wave functions.  The field equation was numerically solved using a hybrid method combining a new type of Chebyshev polynomial and a Legendre wavelet, which provided an efficient and accurate way to approximate the time-dependent wave function.  Two specific potentials, the Coulomb and harmonic oscillators, were examined under this framework, and their wave functions were numerically determined using the same hybrid method.  Furthermore, graphical representations were presented for a generalized Mie-type potential, Coulomb, and harmonic oscillator with specific parameters, offering visual insights into how the fractional parameter affects the probability density function.

We propose a novel perspective on training neural networks, focusing on their ability to generalize effectively. To achieve this, we apply the principles of optimal transport and require the network to satisfy a specific condition - Lipschitz consistency. This condition is met when the network's outputs change at a rate no greater than that of the data distribution. By enforcing this condition as a regularizer, we are able to reduce the complexity of the learned network. This approach is particularly beneficial in scenarios with limited amounts of labeled data. We demonstrate the practical application of this method by utilizing the Hessian of the probability density function, approximated through kernel methods. The resulting model pre-training strategy shows significant improvements in performance across various datasets and neural network architectures.

Can Dialects be preserved by Machine Translation? This research explores whether
neural machine translation (NMT) can be utilized to preserve Dialects. We focus
on Basque, a endangered language with multiple dialects. Basque standards vary
across its standard dialects and its historical variety, Basilebasco. To avoid
skewing data, we divide the Basilebasco corpus into parallel pairs and translate
it to Basque NMT. Unlike prior studies, we don't force the model to mimic the
standard dialects. Instead, we let it capture the Basilebasco consensus. To
achieve this consensus, we utilize different data amounts, model sizes, and
training methods. We compare Basilebasco results to standard dialects. To our
surprise, the Basilebasco system matches or surpasses the standard dialects in
accuracy. This system can be viewed as a form of dialectal translation. To our
knowledge, this is the first study to examine the capability of NMT to capture
variation and preserve minority languages.

Recent observations of the planet HD 80606 b by various types of telescopes, spanning from optical to near-infrared, have produced intriguing results that initially appeared inconsistent with theoretical predictions but were within the margin of error. The planet's highly eccentric orbit presents unique opportunities for the James Webb Space Telescope to make precise measurements that could refine our orbital data. In order to take full advantage of this telescope's capabilities, the primary goal of this study is to create exceptionally accurate orbital predictions for HD 80606 b. In addition, by analyzing transits recorded using a global network of telescopes, we have been able to provide two possible solutions for the planet's orbit based on when future transits and secondary eclipses are expected to occur. On dates spanning from September 2026 to October 2027, both solutions predict that transits will be observable by the James Webb Space Telescope. On dates spanning from May 2027 to January 2028, secondary eclipses will be observable by various types of telescopes only if the primary solution for the planet's orbit holds true. Furthermore, we have demonstrated that combining transits recorded from a global network of telescopes allows us to significantly reduce the margin of error for measurements of the planet's orbit, as opposed to relying on just one observation per transit.

Video games have consistently played a role in rehabilitation over the past three decades, with several scoring frameworks already established for both virtual and physical therapy purposes. However, the diversity of existing game types has created a limitation, as users may face challenges with incorporating certain elements into a therapeutic environment. To address this, a comprehensive review of current game types and their applications in therapy has been undertaken, with the ultimate goal of promoting the use of a gaming framework to facilitate movement relearning in patients with neurological conditions.

This work extends the variational approximation method for driving numerical simulations of phase field functions to functionals defined on piecewise stiff maps. We adapt the Gamma convergence rate of the approximation, while maintaining a bulk term in the energy, similar to Hele-Shaw and Swirling Vortex dynamics. We also discuss the implications of the approximation for the Gamma convergence properties.

We examine the Drell-Yan production of a leptoquark $LQ$ in pairs, specifically focusing on third-generation quark involvement, and begin to explore the potential for $LQ$ decay into a quark and a photon or neutral meson, which could occur beyond the Standard Model. The potential production of these particles could be observed at the LHC or a future hadron collider. To accurately calculate cross-sections for this process, we employ next-to-leading order QCD corrections with consistent parton showers, ensuring color flow preservation. This approach allows for the potential detection of these particles at various colliders, including the LHC with various integration energies, as well as the Future Circular Collider and Future Hadron Collider, based on predicted next-generation machine capabilities.

Radiology patients receive significant radiation during Positron Emission Tomography (PET) scans, prompting the development of reduced-dose techniques to reduce the out-of-distribution effects on medical imaging models trained on reduced-dose images. Reduced-dose PET imaging combines PET and Computerized Tomography (CT) for better image quality, enabling the creation of distributionally robust models that can accurately reduce the reduced-dose PET data to an in-distribution. To achieve this, we introduce a novel approach that utilizes a differentiable projection to create synthetic reduced-dose PET data from CT scans, and a multilayer perceptron to generate reduced-dose PET images from CT scans. By jointly training these models and incorporating uncertainty estimation through multivariate heteroscedastic models, we develop a reduced-dose PET imaging framework that is resilient to reduced-dose data. Our approach outperforms existing methods by reducing root mean square errors and relative volume errors on external test datasets.

This research focuses on Secure Multi-Party Computation (SMPC) for a group of users who wish to jointly train a machine learning model while maintaining data privacy and allowing for system customization. Current SMPC protocols, though effective in ensuring confidentiality, lack flexibility in adapting to the specific requirements of machine learning applications. To address this, we develop a range of customizations within the SMPC framework, including the ability to modify the model architecture, adjust the training algorithm, and incorporate unencrypted data. These customizations are validated through the development of a configurable SMPC prototype, which has been tested in simulations of a collaborative machine learning scenario.

The concept of textual centering, as outlined by the Centering Theory (CT), has significantly influenced our comprehension of language production and processing. 
However, given the advent of neural computational models for coreference resolution, there's a need to reassess the relevance of the CT's key principle within this new framework. 
Our analysis of the neural coreference resolver's (NCR) decision-making process through the lens of the CT's linearization and contextual centering tendencies has been conducted using a specialized corpus of controlled texts specifically created for this purpose. 
By utilizing the Natural Gradient Descent (NDR) framework to examine the NCR's framework, we found that the most influential contextual factor identified in the CT aligns with the concept of "discourse coherence." 
Interestingly, although shorter antecedents are generally considered more central, the most significant cue for the NCR isn't necessarily the most recent mention. 
Furthermore, our findings revealed that the NCR's performance reaches its peak when both the antecedent and mention are situated in the textual foreground. 
The implementation of a neural centering resolver (NCR) that mimics the centering tendencies identified in the experiment led to a substantial reduction in prediction errors by at least 25%. 
This indicates that the aspects of language that a model anticipates aren't always the most critical for accurate mention-centering forecasts.

Graph theory research has a strong interest in the parameterized analysis of graph drawing problems, particularly upward planarity, a subcategory of directed planarity. Upward planarity is NP-complete for general graphs, but there are straightforward, parameterized solutions for specific graph types, such as outerplanar graphs. This paper explores more intricate parameters in relation to different graph types and analyzes the following scenarios: (a) how the maximum clique size affects the parameterized complexity when combined with other clique-containing graph classes, (b) how treewidth and pathwidth individually influence complexity in various decomposition classes, (c) how the number of source-sink transitive edges relates to complexity in different graph types, and (d) the impact of up-arborescence freedom on complexity across various tree-decomposition classes.

Custom frameworks are highly effective in accelerating the development of high-performance machine learning models. However, establishing a new framework from scratch is a time-consuming and intricate process involving multiple steps, from selecting and integrating essential packages to implementing a coherent coding structure. This process is often repeated across various projects, leading many to opt for using existing frameworks with pre-configured environments. Despite the advantages of such frameworks, the complex setup process, typically spanning several hours, can be a significant barrier. This paper introduces the automated setup of a custom machine learning framework using Linux, streamlining the entire process to less than five minutes, as opposed to the usual five to ten hours, notably overcoming the barrier of adopting such a framework for developing performance-critical models.

In the Intorn network, a novel concept called operator expansion is introduced to address the issues of near-neighbors and redundancy. It replaces the traditional Dime's 2-tap operator expansion with a richer set of mathematically interconnected symbols, effectively integrating the graph convolutional network and the intorn convolutional network. This results in the development of Intorn Convolutional Network, a new model that combines the strengths of both models while significantly reducing the total number of parameters and enhancing interpretability through a systematic and coherent feature representation. Extensive experiments conducted on standard graph node classification benchmarks demonstrate that Intorn CNN outperforms existing models, achieving optimal performance with a simplified operator set of just five elements.

In location-based services, determining the proximity of individuals to one another relies on accurate range estimation, which in turn depends on the analysis of signal strength. However, the relationship between received signal strength and range is highly variable and challenging to interpret. Consequently, traditional methods for range estimation are often plagued by inaccuracies. To address this limitation, the present study investigates and proposes utilizing supervised machine learning algorithms in place of conventional approaches, with the objective of enhancing range assessment based on available data. Notably, this study goes beyond conventional machine learning applications by exploring the potential for these algorithms to not only facilitate range assessment but also to provide visualizations of circular zones with improved accuracy.

Theories of modified gravity, specifically $f(R)$ gravity, have attractive features, such as no need for dark matter.  However, they are limited by the requirement of passing a wide range of experimental and observational tests.  In this study, we identify a highly compact object within the framework of a specific $f(R)$ gravity model that appears to be unreasonably dense.  By altering the potential terms in this gravity model, we bypass conflicting regulations.  A whole galaxy would be necessary to match the mass of this object if it were on the threshold of collapsing into a singularity as described by general relativity.  Despite this, we can stabilize it by adding a rotating gas dyson shell around it.  If it were a neutron star, it would be many times smaller than any known neutron star and could not exist under the laws of general relativity.  However, in this $f(R)$ gravity model, it could hold.  If this object were confirmed, the potential terms in this $f(R)$ gravity model would be proven wrong.  Therefore, it could be tested with a gas dyon shell around it.

Network services are allocated and managed through protocols and policies, with their effective use dependent on Service Level Agreements (SLAs). The violation of SLAs triggers misallocation and reduced service reliability. As service networks become more complex, identifying SLA breaches poses a significant challenge. A novel approach is proposed, leveraging peer-to-peer (P2P) technology to monitor and identify SLA breaches through the decentralized, cooperative behavior of network users. This approach is modeled as a game, with the optimal strategy being governed by a decentralized equilibrium. A unique optimal strategy profile, representing the breeding value, can be achieved through a-priori probability adjustments. Based on this approach, the Minimal Cost Breach Identification (MCBI) model is formulated, with its solution providing the optimal breeding value. The features of the P2P-based breach identification method are explored, including robustness, scalability, and anti-manipulability. The approach's performance is evaluated through simulations, leveraging a moving finge best response (MFBR) algorithm to accelerate the convergence of strategies to the breeding value.

The occurrence of beam fragmentation instability in energy recovery linacs is heavily influenced by the shape of the beam current distribution. Simulations of two-pass instability show significant variation in growth rates and mode numbers, but lack concrete validation. A range of beam current distributions was analyzed to further understand this dependency. It was found that energy recovery linacs are particularly susceptible to two-pass beam fragmentation instability due to their inherent design. Field measurements and measurements of beam output at the energy recovery linacs' IP2 reveal a notable correlation between the design and observed instability, indicating a strong correlation coefficient of 0.93. Furthermore, an analytical model's predictions closely match the simulation results and actual observations, with a close correspondence in mode numbers and intrinsic mode numbers, with differences of less than 10%. This agreement is further supported by a proposed definition of a figure of merit, which quantifies the susceptibility of beam fragmentation instability in a design-specific and intuitive manner.

The precise detection of neutrons with a wide energy range and the associated uncertainty remains a significant challenge in the design of neutrino detectors utilizing the neutron cross-section $\chi^2$ test to identify the CH proton-scintillator detector's sensitivity to neutron detection was investigated through the development of an innovative, three-dimensional scintillator sensor with 50% hydrogen content. We simulated the detection capabilities of 1 ton of CH in a 14-meter baseline detector, positioned 10 meters above a conventional $\nu_\mu$ beam, with the CH detector, and determined the relative and absolute uncertainties of the neutron flux measurements. Neutrons with the Carbon residual cross-section were primarily detected as recoil neutrons within a 10-degree angular range, contributing 0.11 (stat) $\pm$ 0.04 (sys) $\phi$ / (10$^\circ$) $^\pm$ 0.21 (beam) uncertainties, while neutrons with the Hydrogen residual cross-section were mostly detected within a 20-degree recoil range, contributing 0.04 $\pm$ 0.04 (rel) uncertainties, with the non-uniformity of the neutron distribution accounting for 0.15 uncertainties. As the midplane of a protoplanetary disc heats up, dust particles begin to undergo chemical transformations. These transformations are influenced by the presence of hydrogen and can alter the way dust particles interact and stick together during the formation of planetary systems. In order to understand this process, we exposed samples of interstellar dust to heat up to 180 Kelvin in a simulated environment that mimics how dust particles experience increasing temperatures in a protoplanetary disc's inner midplane. We then ran experiments with air, vacuum, and various gases such as oxygen and nitrogen to see how these conditions affected the dust samples' properties. Our results indicate that as dust particles heat up in the presence of hydrogen, hydrogen molecules are released from the particles, which can cause them to behave differently and interact with other particles in new ways. This, in turn, can have a significant impact on the formation of planetary systems.

Multi-agent motion planning and control are crucial for the successful operation of collaborative robots in shared human and machine spaces. In the field of broad imitation learning, learning policies that allow robots to replicate human behavior across a wide range of situations is a key objective. This paper introduces an innovative framework for the imitation learning of cooperative motions between multiple agents in a two-player setting, taking into account nonlinear flexibility and barrier evading. This framework adjusts the learning process by minimizing a cost function that measures deviations from desired trajectories, ensuring safety and adaptability in human and machine interactions. 

The proposed framework also includes a five-degree-of-freedom nonlinear rigid constraint to facilitate cooperative behaviors such as passing, following, and passing while maintaining a safe distance. It is applied to pass following passing in a scenario where one agent is evading a barrier. The framework's effectiveness is demonstrated through a set of numerical examples, showing its capability to replicate the behaviors of human drivers in various situations. 

By providing a efficient and accurate method for imitation learning, this framework has the potential to be used in real-world applications, such as autonomous vehicles and other safety-critical systems that require reliable and predictable interactions with humans.

To accurately calculate two-loop form factors of $Q^2$-eigenoperators in N=4 supersymmetric Yang-Mills theory, it is necessary to determine certain multi-leg vertices at the one-loop level. Specifically, we need to determine the central-emission vertex for two gluons, which we have done in this study. By leveraging the dual-conformal symmetry present in this theory, we have used a variety of techniques, including numerical integration, unitarity, and symmetry, to derive a formula for this vertex that is both real and positive. Furthermore, in the limit where the partons are moving in similar directions, this result reduces to a known expression that was obtained using dual-conformal symmetry alone.

Within the Rashba Hubbard model, incorporating a monolayer of atoms with spin-orbit coupling and chemical potential, we examine the impact of an external magnetic field on a system exhibiting in-plane exchange. By incorporating super-orbitals that account for spin-orbit coupling and lattice translation symmetry, we map the Rashba Hubbard Hamiltonian onto an effective four-component Hubbard model. At low temperatures, we utilize the quantum Monte Carlo path integral method to investigate the nature of the superfluid phase transition. Our findings reveal that in the strong in-plane exchange regime, characterized by large in-plane exchange fields, the system exhibits non-Abelian Majorana spin singlet superfluidity, which persists beyond the regime of weak in-plane exchange previously explored.

Using an advanced scanning technique, we have discovered a unique quantum vortex structure in a type II superconductor, specifically in doped $La_{2-x}Sr_xCuO_4$ near its optimal doping level. Our findings reveal the existence of a square-shaped quantum vortex that appears abruptly as some of the vortotice lines intersect at right angles. This phenomenon is quite rare and represents a previously unobserved quantum state. Our data indicates that this square-shaped grid exists in a limited region of the material, occupying about 30% of the d-$BaH_2$ phase space. Moreover, our findings provide valuable insights into the nature of the $d$-wave symmetry of the superconductor and its impact on quantum vortex behavior.

A new model called the bristle polymer model has been developed to model polymer brushes with melted chains. In this model, bases are fixed in a variety of configurations, while chains are considered as having no thickness. In higher dimensions, we show that brushes of elongated polymers create areas that exclude other polymers from the ends, and provide a mathematical understanding of the thickness of these areas using a rescaled version of the Da Prato-Orland model.

Given a graph G and a subset S of its vertices, S is considered a metaset if it uniquely identifies all vertices of G through their distances to elements in S. Furthermore, S is regarded as a shortened metaset if it also minimizes the maximum distance between any node in G and S, equating to the radius of G. In this work, we prove that almost all graphs possess a shortened metric dimension of 1 with the only exception being graphs with a double star structure, where a small set of2 vertices can serve as a shortened metaset.

Recent research utilizing the Fermi-LAT gamma-ray telescope telescope has produced comprehensive all-sky maps, classifying celestial objects and backgrounds across the electromagnetic spectrum. This work leverages the extensive dataset from the telescope to examine the relationship between CMB anisotropy and global object classification. A machine learning algorithm, specifically a gradient boosting decision tree, was trained to classify celestial entities based on gamma-ray flux maps derived from a significant portion of the telescope's observation period. The model's performance showed high accuracy, with areas under the receiver operating characteristic curve exceeding 0.9 for most object types. However, it also identified regions in the sky that exhibit ambiguous classifications and a tendency to misclassify variable objects as blazars. These findings present valuable insights and potential applications for astronomers, including enhancing classification models and facilitating the discovery of new variable objects.

A new mechanism type is now being defined, termed as "rotating serial dictatorship" (RSD), which encompasses all mechanisms that can be mapped to a circular version of serial dictatorship (SD). A specific subclass of RSD, termed "enhanced serial dictatorship" (ESD), has been identified, comprising those mechanisms that surpass SD in welfare while maintaining strategy-proofness. The properties of the ESD class, along with its associated welfare range, are now being explored. Furthermore, the similarities between the welfare ranges of the ESD class and those of the single-crossing environment are being discussed. A novel algorithm, named "dictatorship enhancement" (DE), has been designed to directly transform any given SD into a corresponding ESD, along with its associated welfare range being characterized using this algorithm.

We examined 51 main belt asteroids of carbon-type, ranging in diameter from 14 to 109 kilometers, to identify binary systems within the Pan-STARRS1 PS1. This analysis involved obtaining astrometric measurements across multiple epochs between 2010 and 2013. The results indicate a likelihood of two asteroids, specifically 433 Mirtilla and 66 Maja, to be binary systems with secondary bodies of 39 and 13 kilometers in diameter respectively. These potential binary systems have orbital periods of 3.49 and 0.61 years, and semi-major axes of 0.04 and 0.06 astronomical units. For both systems, we calculated the mass of their secondary bodies as a fraction of their primary, estimated their dark surface albedos, and surface escape velocities. These findings are in line with other known binary asteroids of similar characteristics. It is recommended that further observations using radial velocity or direct imaging be conducted to confirm the existence of these binary systems. This research is part of the PS1 Asteroid Survey within the Pan-STARRS1 Legacy Survey, undertaken using the 1.8-gtelescope and 1.5 wide field camera 1 at the Pan-STARRS1 Observatory in Hawaii.

Machine learning models for regression, particularly those using a linear model with a non-linear neural network, have gained significant popularity due to their computational efficiency and flexible modeling of complex relationships. Researchers typically assess the performance of these algorithms by comparing their estimates to standard linear regression results. However, this comparison can be restrictive when the network data does not conform to partially linear regression assumptions. In such instances, standard estimators may yield biased results, which may be difficult to interpret. In response, we propose an innovative framework for evaluating and utilizing a partially linear regression framework, which involves tailoring the network structure to this framework and assessing its effectiveness through a specific application to social networks. We develop a customized estimator for beta coefficients, which can withstand the complexities of machine learning models, and apply it to an exponential random graph model, a widely used algorithm for social network analysis. Using both simulated and real-world data, we demonstrate the reliability and robustness of our estimator, which outperforms existing alternatives in certain scenarios.
This study introduces a novel form of the Leibniz rule, applicable to the Variable-Order Riemann-Liouville integral and differential operators.

Location-aware venues for outdoor wireless communication have significant potential in providing location-based services, with promising applications in GPS and Wi-Fi positioning. In wireless fingerprinting-based indoor positioning, determining which access points are actively transmitting is crucial for positioning accuracy and efficiency. Both applications rely on identifying spatially organized signals, which can be framed as a subspace estimation problem with missing data. This paper focuses on two widely used sparse subspace estimation algorithms, least-squares and regularized least-squares methods, by analyzing and simplifying their update processes. The analysis of the regularization parameter's impact on algorithm performance is included in the study, with theoretical findings supported by simulation results.

To analyze samples using spectroscopy, scientists rely on processing and visualizing the data. The original version of the open-source RCSEdv visualization tools in Python was released two years ago to help visualizing both imaging and spectral information. A new web-based interface has now been developed in Flask for more intuitive visualization and visualizations can be exported via the new version of the Python library in Python.

The Southern Atlantic Ocean's formation began a North-South separating rift, eventually transforming into the current East-West aligned fissure we see today. This study, utilizing precise plate kinematics and recent seismic data, maps the evolution of the Atlantic plates since the Neogene period. Our analysis indicates the onset of N-S extension in West Africa around 25 million years ago, followed by South America approximately 10 million years later. The breaking point then shifted to the Caribbean around 6 million years ago. At this time, the North American plate started experiencing East-West compression around 25 million years ago, while West Africa and South America remained under N-S stress. The East-West orientation of the Atlantic rift resulted from the rotation of West Africa and South America around the equator due to the pull of the North American plate, creating right-lateral sliding along the equator and N-S tension at higher latitudes. The rotation of West Africa and South America, however, reversed around 10-20 million years ago, bringing the N-S region into the N-E quadrant, where East-West shear produced the Southern and Central Atlantic faults. The East Carpathian fracture, on the other hand, formed from the collision of the African and European plates approximately 25 million years ago, initiating the Alpine orogeny. Evaluations of current methods typically involve assessing their ability to create accurate boundaries between adjacent structures.
